title: Pope Leo in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour
description: Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since havin
body: Pope Leo XIV has told reporters travelling with him to Latin America he is "in pretty good health", in his first comments on his condition since having surgery for lung cancer.The Pope has arrived in Uruguay, the first stop of a 12-day tour which he is undertaking only three weeks after his operation.The pontiff, 71, also said he was "very happy" to be able to make the trip which was thrown into doubt last month when doctors discovered a tumour during a routine scan.The tour will cover Argentina and a much anticipated return to Peru, which the Vatican described as a "homecoming" as the Pope was based there for many years as a missionary, then a bishop."I must confess that, from the very first day, I never had any doubts; I was convinced that this journey had to go forward," the Pope told journalists on his plane to Uruguay. "Thanks to the marvellous medical staff... I believe I am in quite good health," Pope Leo confirmed.Last month's operation to remove a tumour was successful and his doctors say the cancer has not spread.On Friday, he arrived in Monetevideo to a seafront lined with crowds shouting his name as his Popemobile passed.In his first speech of the trip, the Pope said universal healthcare should be "accessible to everyone".He told the crowd in Plaza Independencia the care he received made him think of the "many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis" or receive treatment.He capped his day with a prayer at the Montevideo Cathedral. Pope Leo will cover more than 20,000 miles on his sixth international tour.On Sunday he will travel to Argentina, the homeland of his predecessor Pope Francis who did not return during his own papacy.The Pope said his visit was about being near the people who were looking to the Church for a message of "hope".

schema.headline: Pope Leo in 'pretty good health' as he starts Latin America tour

title: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
description: Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago Peña over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.He has been
body: Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago Peña over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.Peña, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal."Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent."It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".

schema.headline: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest

title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge
description: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida after being c
body: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.Markle, 82, was arrested in Florida on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said. He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the DoJ said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies". In a 30-minute court hearing on Friday he was also ordered to submit to electronic monitoring, but no plea was taken.At the court hearing, the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.He was brought into court in a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest. Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle. "Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said. He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide". Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country. Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr. Markle Sr moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was then reportedly living in a Florida rehabilitation centre learning to walk again after having his leg amputated.In October, London's Metropolitan Police confirmed that it had received a letter in 2019 making a "number of claims" relating to Markle Sr. The Met said information contained in the letter, which related to allegations against Meghan's father outside the UK, was passed on to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but it did not share it with other law enforcement agencies. The force has since voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IPOC) over its handling of the letter. In a statement released in October after the allegations against Markle Sr emerged, the Duchess of Sussex said: "I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year.

schema.headline: Meghan's father Thomas Markle under house arrest after child sex abuse material charge

title: Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE
description: The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.The move by John Whitmire, a Demo
body: The mayor of Houston, Texas, has directed the city's police to limit co-operation with federal immigration officials.The move by John Whitmire, a Democrat, comes on the heels of stunning victories by the party in Texas during this week's midterm elections. It breaks with policy set by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid. "I do this to begin a healing process," Whitmire said on Friday, and to "reduce fear and anxiety across our community". He added: "I also do this knowing that elections matter."There has been months of public outcry in Houston after an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer fatally shot a man who was driving to work. Houston police chief Noe Diaz said on Friday that officers will now only contact ICE if someone they arrest for a jailable offence also has an administrative ICE warrant, which are issued internally by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), within which ICE operates."For example, if our police officers pull someone over for a minor traffic infraction and they write a citation, that person receives a citation and goes about their day," Diaz said. Under the previous rules, Houston police officers were required to inform ICE if anyone they were dealing with came up as having one of these warrants attached to their name when they were searched on the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) - a digital database that includes records on wanted persons, stolen property, certain missing people and those arrested and fingerprinted for serious offences.Whitmire said on Friday that he had directed the Houston Police Department to make the changes through an executive order. He also called on Congress to change federal immigration rules, saying "ICE needs better training. They need body cameras. They need to be trained in de-escalation."He added, "But this can only be done in Washington. I can only control what I can control."In response, a spokesperson for the DHS told Houston's NBC affiliate, KPRC 2, in a statement: "We remain disappointed that sanctuary politicians seek to limit cooperation with ICE, as our law enforcement are simply fulfilling their sworn duties to serve and protect our communities." "Partnerships with law enforcement are critical to having the resources we need to arrest criminal illegal aliens across the country," the spokesperson added.Another Texas city, Austin, has also begun implementing a similar policy change. Democrats won both the US Senate and House of Representatives in Tuesday's midterms, taking control of Congress for the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.Texas, a long-time Republican stronghold, was the site of one of the most stunning upsets in the vote, with the state electing its first Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa, as the first Democrat governor since 1995. It also elected its first Democratic senator since 1988.Whitmire has previously faced criticism for abiding by immigration enforcement policies under the Trump administration. He had resisted previous calls to implement similar changes over concerns that the White House could send a surge of immigration officials in response. , externalAbbott has also threatened to take pull  millions in funds from  cities like Houston, Dallas and Austin unless they allow police to cooperate fully with federal immigration officials. The BBC has contacted Abbott's office for comment.Whitmire's announcement comes a week after an ICE officer was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after he allegedly hit a man with a vehicle in Texas.Earlier this year, large protests broke out in Houston after an ICE officer fatally shot a man driving to work.The deceased, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old Mexican national who lived in the US as an undocumented immigrant for decades, was not the intended target, officials said after the incident.

schema.headline: Texas mayor instructs police to limit co-operation with ICE

title: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values
description: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock val
body: Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday, ending the day up 1.1%, partly reversing some of its 5.5% fall. The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI."The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today."I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure."The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said. "We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained."Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."

schema.headline: AI stocks bounce back after trillions wiped from market values

title: Diwali 2026: Indians celebrate festival with lights and fireworks
description: Millions across India are celebrating Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colour
body: Millions across India are celebrating Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.Air pollution in the Indian capital Delhi has reached such hazardous levels that it is the most polluted Diwali festival in a decade. New measures to improve air quality do not seem to have been successful.India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks. In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% fewer emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are at reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.

schema.headline: Diwali 2026: Indians celebrate festival with lights and fireworks

title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, says Barnier
description: The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy B
body: The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago.But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access.He said there was not a "single market à la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt.Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms"."There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market."Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit.Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime. Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum.Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll.Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point.He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship.Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member.The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises."Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. It was a lie".The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent £350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead". Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly £350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS". Critics have said that the £350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's £75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK.Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the £350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise. ​In his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only £175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money".Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the £350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth."

schema.headline: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, says Barnier

title: Poland shooting: Surgeon who assisted wounded police officer 'undoubtedly saved his life'
description: Surgeon having lunch near Krakow shooting undoubtedly saved officer's life, colleague saysFigure caption, Watch: Doctor who treated victims of Krakow
body: Surgeon having lunch near Krakow shooting undoubtedly saved officer's life, colleague saysFigure caption, Watch: Doctor who treated victims of Krakow shooting speaks to the BBCByOlivia Ireland and Nathan WilliamsOne of two surgeons who treated victims on the streets in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer.The pair were eating near the city's Main Market Square on Saturday when a gunman began firing at random, killing six people and injuring 15.The doctors raced to treat both the attacker and two officers shot while subduing the perpetrator.On Sunday, the officers - both hailed as "true heroes" by the prime minister for preventing further deaths - emerged from comas.Prosecutors launched a terror investigation after ministers previously said the 24-year-old Polish attacker - who remains in a critical condition - was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies". A British national and Austrian woman were among those killed alongside four Poles.Professor Michal Pędziwiatr was having lunch with a colleague, named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, and their families in central Krakow when they heard gunshots.Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible. "We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around."Figure caption, What we know about the deadly Krakow shootingHe said his colleague used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most injured policeman, allowing them to wait for an ambulance which transferred the officer to hospital.Pędziwiatr said they came to learn that one of those they treated was the apparent attacker. "As a doctor... it doesn't matter to me if it's a victim or a suspect," he said. "It's not our task to decide what to do with this guy... for us, it was another heavily injured victim, that's all."According to local media, Wierdak is a renowned surgeon in Krakow. The University Hospital in Krakow states Pędziwiatr is head of General, Oncological, Metabolic and Emergency Surgery.The police officers have been identified as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański.Image source, Getty ImagesThe attacker has not yet been named by authorities.When his house was searched after the attack in central Krakow, the bodies of his parents and sister were found.The National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland launched an investigation into the attack with a unit specialising in "terrorist offences" taking the lead.Separately, reports emerged that six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers also assisted in the aftermath of the shooting.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Investigations continued in central Krakow on Sunday before Main Market Square reopened James McConnell, an officer, told RTE News the group were on a city break and were close to the main square, external when the shooting happened. The volunteers who are trained to provide medical care immediately sought to help injured people, providing "CPR and haemorrhage control".Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded.Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives".Not knowing where the gunman was - or if there was more than one - they "just kept sprinting", eventually finding a hotel to hide inside.Figure caption, How the deadly shooting in Krakow unfoldedTom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover"."I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away," he said.The suspect wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces.Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said "everything suggests" the suspect was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held ultra-nationalist views.The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) on Saturday in the historic centre of Krakow.Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out.The glass fronts of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes.The mayor of Krakow said he had submitted an urgent request for the two officers injured while stopping the attacker to be awarded titles of honorary citizens of the city.Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.

schema.headline: Poland shooting: Surgeon who assisted wounded police officer 'undoubtedly saved his life'

title: NZ election: Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver tightest election in years
description: New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather."It's pret
body: New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather."It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread.""Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits."I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further. "Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions. A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate. But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party – the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's decline accelerated into a dive during the Covid pandemic. Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to:  finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs. But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview."It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened."The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home. High inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries – set by a supermarket duopoly – is among the highest in the developed world.And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July."There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.Increasingly polarised public debate – around topics like Māori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration – have added to the mental load for many in those communities."There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day – a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and even their parents have considered moving to Australia."It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.Many of these issues affecting New Zealand are global trends - and it's undeniable that Kiwis' standard of living is better than many others.But these issues are having a corrosive impact on its national identity."It leads to a crisis of confidence about what New Zealand is and where it's going," Helen Clark, who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, tells the BBC.Her foundation surveys New Zealanders every year about social cohesion, and its most recent report found Kiwis - in particular young people - feel far more isolated than they did a generation ago, attitudes towards multiculturalism are souring and the population is becoming less hopeful.Faith in institutions and leaders has taken an alarming turn: only two out of five New Zealanders trust the government to do the right thing, while less than half of the country trusts the courts."There's a feeling that, really, there's no-one who cares," Clark says.

schema.headline: NZ election: Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver tightest election in years

title: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat
description: Figure caption, Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last monthByBethany Bellin BavariaPerched on a ridge high up in the
body: Figure caption, Fire engulfed Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat in Bavaria last monthByBethany Bellin BavariaPerched on a ridge high up in the spectacular scenery of the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house called The Eagle's Nest, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany's Nazi past.Known in German as Kehlsteinhaus, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938, and frequented by Adolf Hitler and other high-ranking Nazis and their guests. After World War Two it was classified as a historical monument recalling the Nazi era.Last month it was gutted by fire in a suspected arson attack, and some believe it should be completely destroyed, the site returned to nature and all memory of its Nazi past forgotten.But others want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a site for Neo-Nazi pilgrimage at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right.Germany has an "everlasting responsibility to communicate, to deal with our Nazi past", said Isabel Heinemann, professor of contemporary history at Munich's Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität (LMU).But rebuilding the site completely, she warned, would mean putting "highly ideologised or highly ideological architecture" back in place.Image source, Galerie Bilderwelt/Getty ImagesImage caption, Adolf Hitler used the mountain retreat to welcome guestsBefore it was burned down during the evening of 23 October, the Eagle's Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant.Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden.Once there, they could eat sausages in the beer garden on the Obersalzberg at 1,834m (6,017ft) above sea level, overlooking the Alps.Unlike Hitler's nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War Two and demolished in 1952, the Eagle's Nest survived the war.Tens of thousands of tourists visited each season, providing an important source of income to the region.In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by.Image source, Universal Images Group via Getty ImagesImage caption, Before it was burned down, the Kehlsteinhaus or Eagle's Nest had long been a tourist destination in BavariaAround 15 years ago, a photo exhibit was opened in the Kehlsteinhaus about its history.Although the Eagle's Nest itself was "largely destroyed" by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed.The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained in a secure psychiatric hospital on suspicion of arson.Some feel this is the moment to allow the site to fade into history."It's been torched now. It's been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state," said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge.That has happened with "quite a few other Nazi sites", he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself: "The bunker was filled in with concrete and a children's playground put on the top of it on the ground."The Kehlsteinhaus was just "a Nazi vanity project" since romanticised by the name Eagle's Nest, he said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police say the old Nazi retreat was largely destroyed by last month's fireBut Bavaria's authorities take a different view about the site's future.Both the state's interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus."We can hardly leave a ruin standing there," Herrmann said.Sven Keller, head of the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, believes it is important not to leave the site in ruins, as that could encourage Neo-Nazi pilgrims, who would be able to hike up there completely undisturbed."We have quite some experience at Obersalzberg with what happens if we clear those sites. Hitler's Berghof was demolished in the 1950s, and in our experience, this does not remove such sites from the mental maps of people," he told the BBC's Today programme.Nor does he believe "a one-on-one reconstruction" of the site is possible, and Blume has made clear on Bavarian radio that "it should not and must not cost the taxpayer anything".Image source, ERIC SCHWAB/AFPImage caption, After Hitler's downfall, US soldiers captured the mountain-top retreat and are seen relaxing here on 4 May 1945Herrmann said they would look for a sensible solution in consultation with historians, given the historically complex circumstances surrounding the building.Heinemann, who also heads the Leibniz Institute for Contemporary History, believes full-scale reconstruction should be "out of the question"."I rather think we can document the state left by the fire and also document the historical remains of the Kehlsteinhaus, and then reconstruct parts in a modern design, to make clear the different layers of time that can be seen in this building," she told the BBC.Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era. With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency.A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban "stumbling stones" memorials - embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis.In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used.The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi pilgrims.But others had wanted the house to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past.As one resident of Braunau am Inn told me, it was a delicate balance between how much to remember and how much to forget.

schema.headline: Germans wrestle with what to do with Hitler's destroyed Eagle's Nest retreat

title: Mogadishu tourism: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees her city
description: As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.This
body: As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. Welcome to... Mogadishu.This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital.Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture.Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes."It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.The dunes, she adds, remind some visitors of the Sahara. But her tours are about more than scenic views. She also takes visitors to the fish market, where they discover the variety of marine life available along Somalia's extensive coastline and to parts of the city that reflect its history as a busy Indian Ocean trading centre, with the influences of both its Ottoman and Italian former rulers.Visitors can also sample Somali food, including camel meat, samosas and traditional tea.Sucdi says many arrive in the city with expectations shaped by years of hearing about the insecurity."Mostly, they are surprised by how beautiful the country is and how welcoming people are," she says.At the fish market, she says, visitors are particularly impressed by the variety of fish species.Tourism remains a relatively new field in Somalia, she says, with only a handful working as guides in Mogadishu.The business is seasonal, but Sucdi says this year has been particularly encouraging, although numbers are still fairly low. Having five tourists a week is considered a success but she is confident that numbers will grow.However, she says many visitors are still concerned about security.Since the collapse of Somalia's central government in 1991, Mogadishu has endured decades of civil war, destruction and displacement. Much of the city centre was reduced to rubble, and basic services and infrastructure largely broke down.But following the withdrawal of the Islamist militant group al-Shabab from most of the city in 2011, and the establishment of the federal government in 2012, Mogadishu has undergone a gradual transformation. Returning members of the Somali diaspora, local entrepreneurs and investors helped fuel a construction boom, with new hotels, restaurants, businesses and residential developments reshaping the capital. Today, Mogadishu is a growing commercial hub, although insecurity and the legacy of conflict remain part of everyday life.About 10,000 tourists visited Somalia in 2024, a 50% increase on the previous year, according to the country's tourism department.Many visitors ask about their safety before travelling and often encounter security checkpoints around the city.But she says their experience on the ground is generally positive."What they heard from the news and everywhere else is not the same as what they see in the country," she says.Although some question whether Mogadishu is safe enough for a young woman to be working as a tour guide, Sucdi is determined to continue.She wants visitors to experience a Somalia that is rarely seen."I would want them to see the beautiful, welcoming side of Mogadishu, and not the side that they heard from the media, which is explosions and bombs," she says.Somalia has Africa's longest mainland coastline, stretching more than 3,000km (1,860 miles) along the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.Its beaches and sand dunes sit alongside historic coastal cities such as Mogadishu, whose culture reflects centuries of Indian Ocean trade.For some tourists, that contrast between the country's reputation and what they experience can be striking.American travel content creator Chris Reese, who goes by the name Authentic Travelling, has visited Mogadishu twice. His first trip, almost a year ago, was a solo visit. He enjoyed it so much that he decided to return with a group of friends, who had seen videos of his visit on social media."I had such a positive experience - I really enjoyed seeing the country for the first time - that I opted to bring back a group of my friends," he says.What stands out for Chris is the city's coastal setting, its food and atmosphere."It is such a beautiful tropical place. I love the vibe, the weather and the food," he says.During the group's visit, they enjoy lunch overlooking the Indian Ocean before heading out to explore the beaches and sand dunes."The desert is beautiful and picturesque. It is also amazing that it's barely a 30-minute drive from Mogadishu," he says.Before his first trip, Chris says, much of what he knew about Somalia came from international news coverage."If you only read the news reports about Somalia, you would be scared to visit. And honestly, that's what I saw in the media before I came, mostly negative headlines."But visiting the country challenged those perceptions."Coming here, on my very first trip, showed me that there is so much more to this country than what is shown in the headlines," he says.Mihaela Patap, from Romania, loves Somalia's natural beauty.Although she has spent only a few hours in Mogadishu, she has already visited the sand dunes and taken in the Indian Ocean coastline."The desert was so beautiful to see. I have also enjoyed the beach, and the ocean. It is inspiring," she says.Having travelled to Somalia from neighbouring Ethiopia, she says she has been struck by the people's friendliness."I don't see anything dangerous. I feel safe and the people are warm," she says.An experienced traveller, Mihaela says she prefers to visit new countries without having preconceived ideas."I travel the world to see new places, to see countries, to see the differences. I don't take a picture in my mind to compare the reality with. I'm just expecting the new to come to me," she says.She hopes to share her experience and encourage others to visit Somalia."I'm going to post my pictures and say good things about what I'm experiencing. I'm going to promote it," she says.For Sucdi, that potential is personal. She is continuing a family profession while building a business in an industry with few women and using digital platforms to reach audiences far beyond Mogadishu."Somalia still has a long way to go before tourism becomes a major industry," she says.  "Through my tours, I am giving visitors an opportunity to experience its landscapes, our culture and people beyond the familiar negative headlines."For her, every visitor is another opportunity to tell a fuller story of Mogadishu.

schema.headline: Mogadishu tourism: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees her city

title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that po
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByDaniel BushWashington correspondent and Madeline HalpertRepublicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy."There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away. It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency."There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist. "But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."Image source, Getty ImagesShould Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decadesDemocrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination."Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nominationOther rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race."It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said."But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."Figure caption, 'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shiftFollow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. title: Iran executes three men for 'armed unrest' after January protests
description: Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.Hassan Dioband, H
body: Iran has executed three men accused of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media.Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in the city of Karaj, west of Tehran, Iran's state news agency Tasnim, external reported.The executions are the latest in a series linked to the protests, including those of people accused of having ties to Israel and the United States.The number of executions in Iran has increased since US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic began in late February.The protest movement initially sparked in December last year by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 of January.Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, and blamed the violence on "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the US and Israel.However foreign-based NGOs gave higher figures and the BBC received multiple accounts from Iranians of security forces opening fire on unarmed protesters.Tasnim reported that the three men were executed after the Supreme Court upheld their convictions and found them guilty of "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups".The damage allegedly included an electricity substation in Karaj which caused power outages in some areas.Dioband was arrested on 11 January after investigations identified him as a suspect in attacks on public property and incitement to violence.Ten others accused of taking part in the unrest under his supervision were later arrested.Reuters news agency reports that they received prison terms of 5 to 10 years.The latest executions in Iran come after the UN human rights chief Volker Türk said he was alarmed by the rise in death penalties.In August, Türk said at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests.Iran is thought to be the world's second-most prolific executioner after China. Last year, it put to death at least 2,159 people, according to Amnesty International.The human rights group said that was the highest figure on record since 1981 and included 45 executions of suspected dissidents on national security-related charges.

schema.headline: Iran executes three men for 'armed unrest' after January protests

title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
description: Figure caption, Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in EgyptByEmer MoreauAt least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egypti
body: Figure caption, Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in EgyptByEmer MoreauAt least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment. Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Uninjured passengers and bystanders searched derailed carriages for injured peopleThe government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.The Egyptian Red Crescent said it was providing aid and psychological support to victims and their families at the scene.The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.Image source, Getty ImagesTrains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains. The railway authority has not said how long it expects this to take.The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.Foreign leaders and dignitaries have shared condolences and support for the victims.Saudi Arabia's ministry of foreign affairs expressed "solidarity" with Egypt and wished those hurt a speedy recovery.Turkey's ambassador to Egypt wrote on X that he extended "heartfelt condolences and sincere sympathy" to the victims, their families, and the Egyptian people.

schema.headline: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt

title: With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentIn the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Dona
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByNorth America correspondentIn the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job."The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests."Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."Figure caption, Watch: Trump says he appointed Stephen Miller ‘to make a change’Miller is best known for being the driving force behind the Trump administration's aggressive immigration enforcement policies, which has included ramping up funding for enforcement operations across the US.He made headlines when he called Alex Pretti, who was shot and killed by federal immigration officials during a massive deportation operation in Minneapolis, a "domestic terrorist" and an "assassin". He would later walk back those words, saying federal agents "may not have been following" proper protocol.He has also reportedly played a leading role in the US military operations in Venezuela and against suspected drug trafficking operations in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which critics have condemned as extra-judicial killings.Miller joined Trump's political operation early in his 2016 presidential bid as a strategist and incendiary warm-up speaker at his raucous campaign rallies.He was one of the few senior White House staffers to persevere through the entirety of his first term. He stayed loyal to Trump during his political exile following attempts to overturn his ballot-box defeat in 2020 failed. He then returned in the influential role of deputy chief of staff for policy in Trump's second term.Wiles, who co-managed the president's successful 2024 re-election campaign, developed a reputation as a cool professional who avoided the White House staffing upheavals, dramatic policy reversals and personality clashes that typified Trump's first presidential term.The president, however, began souring on Wiles in recent months, as his political standing in the US declined, culminating in Tuesday's electoral rout. He also reportedly chafed at news stories indicating that those in Wiles' orbit were landing lucrative consulting jobs through their connections to the president.Figure caption, What has Stephen Miller’s role been in Trump’s second term?Miller's hardline views sets up clash with CongressWhile Trump praised Miller's effectiveness as a manager on Friday, working with Congress could prove to be a challenge.It is difficult to overstate how disliked Miller is by most Democrats – and some Republicans."Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands," Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries wrote on X.  "His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor."Earlier this year, Miller posted on social media that James Talarico, who had just secured the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in Texas, was "their first transgender Senate candidate".The Democratic Party offered a terse, obscenity laced reply, telling Miller to shut up.Now Miller will have to negotiate with a US Senate that includes a newly elected Talarico as one of its rising stars, after an election in which polls found that 58% of voters believe the administration's immigration enforcement actions had "gone too far" and Hispanics decisively turned against Republican candidates.Image source, Getty ImagesOn Wednesday, in a social media post attempting to explain the Republican midterm defeats, Vice-President JD Vance - who is an early frontrunner for the Republican 2028 presidential nomination - wrote that he was "open to the idea that we should change enforcement - by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labour, for instance".That now seems less likely with an immigration hardline taking the White House helm.Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican senator who is retiring at the end of the year, has been particularly vocal in condemning Miller. He has called him "incompetent" and "the architect of some of the dumbest proposals from the Trump White House".Other Republicans, however, have sung his praises."Stephen Miller has been a true conservative warrior since his days as a Senate staffer, a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness, and a steadfast fighter for President Trump for over a decade," Utah Senator Mike Lee posted on X after Trump's announcement.At a time when congressional Democrats are promising to launch new investigations and oversight into the Trump administration, it appears that a "warrior" and a "fighter" is the kind of person the president wants to have running his White House.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter.
